meta.title: How Electricity Reaches Your Home
meta.subtitle: From the power plant to the socket, one step at a time
meta.description: Follow the journey of electricity: how it is generated, why it travels at high voltage, how the grid keeps supply and demand balanced, and what happens inside your home's electrical panel. No prior knowledge needed.
learningObjectives: Explain how a generator turns motion into electricity
Describe why transmission lines use high voltage
Name the main parts of the power grid and what each does
Read the basic information on an electricity bill

sections.title: Generating electricity
sections.summary: Where electricity comes from and how motion becomes current.

blocks.text:
Electricity is the flow of [[electric charge]]. In a copper wire, tiny particles called [[electron|electrons]] are pushed along the metal, a bit like water pushed through a pipe. They can only keep flowing around a closed loop, called an [[electric circuit|circuit]].

Two quantities describe that flow:

- [[voltage]] is the *push* that drives the charge;
- [[current]] is *how much* charge flows each second.

blocks.title: The water analogy
blocks.text: Think of voltage as water pressure and current as the amount of water flowing through the pipe.

check.prompt: In the water analogy, what does voltage correspond to?
check.explanation: Voltage is the push; current is the amount that flows.

visual.caption: From steam, water or wind to electric current

blocks.text:
Power plants turn other forms of [[energy]] into electricity, and almost all of them work the same way: something spins a [[turbine]], and the turbine turns a [[generator]].

Inside the generator, magnets rotate next to coils of wire. A moving magnetic field pushes the electrons in the wire: this is called [[electromagnetic induction]].

visual.title: Illustrative electricity supply of a European country
visual.caption: Example figures for teaching purposes; real shares vary by country and year.

blocks.text:
Power plants use different [[energy source|energy sources]]. Some are [[renewable energy|renewable]] (sun, wind, water), others burn [[fossil fuel|fossil fuels]] such as natural gas.

The combination of sources a country uses is called its [[energy mix]].

glossary.definition: A property of particles such as electrons; moving charge is what we call electricity.
The 'push' that drives electric charge through a circuit, measured in volts (V).
The amount of electric charge flowing per second, measured in amperes (A).
A wheel with blades that spins when steam, water or wind flows through it.
A machine that converts rotation into electricity using magnets and coils of wire.
The creation of a voltage in a wire when the magnetic field around it changes.
Anything used to produce electricity: sun, wind, water, gas, coal, uranium and so on.
Energy from sources that naturally replenish, such as sunlight, wind and flowing water.
The share of each energy source in the electricity a country produces or consumes.
A tiny particle with a negative electric charge; moving electrons carry electricity through metal wires.
A closed loop of conductors through which current can flow from a source, through devices, and back.
The ability to do work, such as moving, heating or lighting something. Electrical energy is measured in kilowatt-hours on bills.
Coal, oil or natural gas: fuels formed over millions of years from ancient plants and animals, which release carbon dioxide when burned.

sections.title: The power grid
sections.summary: How the power grid carries electricity hundreds of kilometres and delivers it at the right voltage.

visual.caption: Typical voltages in a European grid (exact values vary by country).

blocks.text: The [[power grid|grid]] carries electricity from power plants to homes. Its wires heat up when [[current]] flows through them, and that heat is wasted energy. The loss grows with the *square* of the current.

blocks.caption: Power lost in a wire: current squared times the wire's resistance.

blocks.text: Here *R* is the wire's [[resistance]]. Electrical [[power]] equals voltage times current (P = V × I), so the grid can deliver the same power with less current by raising the [[voltage]]: [[transmission]] lines run at hundreds of thousands of volts. A [[transformer]] changes the voltage up or down.

steps.title: Step-up substation
steps.description: A transformer raises it to 220–380 kV.

steps.title: Transmission
steps.description: Long-distance lines carry it across the country.

steps.title: Step-down substation
steps.description: Voltage is lowered for local distribution.

steps.title: Distribution
steps.description: Local lines and a final transformer bring 230 V to homes.

blocks.text: After transmission, [[substation|substations]] lower the voltage and local [[distribution]] networks bring it to neighbourhoods. A last transformer, often in a small cabin on your street, brings it to 230 V.

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  P[Power plant] --> U[Step-up substation]
  U --> T[Transmission lines]
  T --> D[Step-down substation]
  D --> L[Distribution lines]
  L --> H[Homes]
blocks.caption: The same journey as a diagram.

blocks.text: Electricity is hard to store in large amounts, so production must match consumption second by second. The grid uses [[alternating current]], and the [[grid operator]] watches its [[frequency]], 50 Hz in Europe, to know if supply and demand are balanced.

rows: Asks plants or batteries to produce more
blocks.caption: Frequency is the grid's balance indicator.

check.prompt: If more electricity is consumed than produced, grid frequency rises.
check.explanation: When demand exceeds supply, the generators slow down slightly and frequency drops.

glossary.definition: Moving electricity over long distances at very high voltage.
A device that raises or lowers voltage without moving parts.
A facility with transformers and switches that connects parts of the grid at different voltages.
The local network that delivers electricity from substations to homes and businesses.
The organisation that runs the grid and keeps supply and demand balanced.
How many complete back-and-forth cycles alternating current makes each second, measured in hertz (Hz). At 50 Hz the current reverses direction 100 times per second.
The network of power plants, power lines, substations and transformers that carries electricity to consumers.
The rate at which electrical energy is delivered or used, measured in watts (W). It equals voltage times current.
How strongly a material opposes the flow of current, measured in ohms (Ω). Higher resistance turns more energy into heat.
Electric current that regularly reverses direction. Grids use it because transformers only work with alternating current.

sections.title: Electricity at home
sections.summary: The meter, the panel and the numbers on your bill.

highlights.label: Meter
highlights.description: Measures how much energy you use.

highlights.label: Main switch
highlights.description: Cuts power to the whole home.

highlights.label: Residual current device
highlights.description: Trips if current leaks, for example through a person.

blocks.text: Electricity enters the home through the [[electricity meter]]. From there it reaches the [[electrical panel|panel]], where a [[main switch]], a [[residual current device]] and several [[circuit breaker|circuit breakers]] protect people and wiring.
Never open the electrical panel's cover yourself: any work inside it must be done by a qualified electrician.

Your bill charges for [[energy consumption]], measured in [[kilowatt-hour|kilowatt-hours]] (kWh), plus fixed charges for using the [[power grid|grid]] and taxes. Energy used equals [[power]] multiplied by time.

blocks.title: Quick calculation
blocks.text: A 2 [[kilowatt|kW]] oven used for 1.5 hours consumes 2 × 1.5 = 3 kWh.

check.prompt: A 1 kW heater runs for 4 hours. How much energy does it use?
check.explanation: Energy = power × time = 1 kW × 4 h = 4 kWh.

glossary.definition: The device that measures the electrical energy a home consumes.
A safety switch that cuts power when it detects current leaking to earth.
A switch that opens automatically when a circuit carries too much current.
The total electrical energy used over a period of time.
The energy used by a 1 kW device running for one hour; the unit on electricity bills.
The box where the home's wiring is split into circuits, each protected by its own breaker.
The switch in the electrical panel that turns off the power to the whole home at once.
A unit of power equal to 1,000 watts.

questions.prompt: What does a turbine do in a power plant?

options.text: It spins and turns the generator

questions.explanation: Steam, water or wind spins the turbine, which rotates the generator.

questions.prompt: Electromagnetic induction creates a voltage when the magnetic field around a wire changes.
questions.explanation: This is the principle every generator relies on.

questions.prompt: Which of these are renewable energy sources?
questions.explanation: Wind, sun and water replenish naturally; natural gas is a fossil fuel.

options.text: how much charge flows each second
the energy used in an hour

questions.explanation: Current is the flow rate of charge, measured in amperes.

questions.prompt: Why do transmission lines use very high voltage?

options.text: To lower the current and reduce losses
Because generators cannot produce low voltage

questions.explanation: Losses grow with the square of the current, so higher voltage and lower current waste less energy.

questions.prompt: Put the journey of electricity in order.
questions.explanation: Voltage is raised for transmission, then lowered again before reaching homes.

questions.prompt: In Europe the grid frequency is 50 Hz.
questions.explanation: European grids run at 50 Hz; North America uses 60 Hz.

questions.prompt: What device changes the voltage between parts of the grid?
What does a residual current device protect against?

options.text: Current leaking to earth, for example through a person

questions.explanation: It trips when it detects a leak, which can save lives.

questions.prompt: A 500 W lamp stays on for 10 hours. How much energy does it use?
